hints: Write the expected $3d$ and $4s$ occupancies for Cr, Mn and Fe from atomic numbers 24, 25 and 26, remembering that $4s$ fills before $3d$ when building up.
Recall why Cr is anomalous with a half filled $3d$ subshell, and apply Hund's rule to count singly occupied orbitals in $3d^5$ versus $3d^6$.
walkthrough:
Build the isolated atom configurations**
Think of isolated gaseous atoms, not ions. Mn is $\text{[Ar]} 3d^5 4s^2$ and Fe is $\text{[Ar]} 3d^6 4s^2$. Cr is the special one, it promotes one $4s$ electron to gain a half filled $3d$ shell, so $\text{[Ar]} 3d^5 4s^1$. That promotion is stabilised by exchange energy.

Count unpaired electrons with Hund's rule**
In $3d$, each of the five orbitals takes one electron before pairing. So $3d^5$ gives 5 unpaired for both Cr and Mn. For Fe, $3d^6$ means five singly occupied plus one paired, leaving 4 unpaired. In $4s$ there is only one orbital, so $4s^1$ gives 1 unpaired for Cr, while $4s^2$ is paired and gives 0 for Mn and Fe.

Final answer: 3d unpaired: Cr 5, Mn 5, Fe 4.
4s unpaired: Cr 1, Mn 0, Fe 0.

hints: List the three named products and work out their formulae, noting that potassium manganate(VI) contains $\text{MnO}_4^{2-}$ and the colourless gas from heating a Group 1 oxoanion is usually $\text{O}_2$.
Balance Mn and K first by using 2 $\text{KMnO}_4$, then check O atoms balance with the $\text{O}_2$ formed.
walkthrough:
Translate names to formulae**
Potassium manganate(VI) is $\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4$ because Mn(VI) in $\text{MnO}_4^{2-}$ needs two $\text{K}^+$. Manganese(IV) oxide is $\text{MnO}_2$. The colourless gas evolved on strong heating of this oxidiser is oxygen, $\text{O}_2$.

Balance the equation**
You start with $\text{KMnO}_4$. You need K and Mn to balance across $\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4$ and $\text{MnO}_2$. Using $2\text{KMnO}_4$ gives 2 K and 2 Mn on each side. Oxygen then balances: 8 O on left, $4 + 2 + 2 = 8$ O on right, so $2\text{KMnO}_4 \rightarrow \text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4 + \text{MnO}_2 + \text{O}_2$.

hints: Picture the five $3d$ orbitals in the free ion as degenerate, then think what ligands approaching along axes do to their energies.
Consider what happens when white light shines on the complex and an electron can jump the small gap between the split $d$ levels.
Link the colour you see to the colour absorbed, remembering the observed colour is what is left over, not what is absorbed.
walkthrough:
Split the d orbitals**
In a free transition metal ion the five $3d$ orbitals have the same energy. When ligands bond, their lone pairs repel $d$ electrons unequally, so the set splits into a lower energy group and a higher energy group with a small gap corresponding to visible light energy.

Promote an electron with light**
If the ion has a partly filled $d$ subshell, an electron in the lower set can absorb a photon of visible light and jump to a vacant orbital in the upper set. This is a $d$-$d$ transition. Fully filled or empty $d$ subshells cannot do this, which is why this explains colour only for most transition complexes.

See the complementary colour**
White light minus the absorbed wavelength is what reaches your eye. So if red is absorbed, you see green-blue. That transmitted or reflected mixture is the complementary colour of the absorbed light.

Final answer: Ligands cause the $d$ orbitals to split into two energy levels.
Electrons absorb visible light to be promoted to the higher $d$ level.
The colour observed is the complementary colour to that absorbed.

hints: Recall the classic pale blue precipitate formed when $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ is added to $\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ and how many $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands are replaced by $\text{OH}^-$.
Think what excess $\text{NH}_3$ does to that precipitate by ligand substitution, giving a deep blue solution with four $\text{NH}_3$ ligands.
For reaction 4, identify the salt formed when a carbonate reacts with ethanoic acid, keeping Cu(II) with ethanoate anions.
walkthrough:
Identify precipitate A**
$\text{OH}^-$ deprotonates coordinated water in a precipitation reaction. Two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands are replaced to give the neutral pale blue $\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4\text{(OH)}_2\text{]}$, often simplified as $\text{Cu(OH)}_2$.

Identify complex B**
Excess $\text{NH}_3$ acts as a stronger ligand and redissolves the precipitate by substitution. Four $\text{NH}_3$ replace four waters to give the deep blue $\text{[Cu(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$.

Identify compound C**
$\text{CuCO}_3$ plus ethanoic acid is an acid carbonate reaction giving the copper(II) salt of the acid, so copper(II) ethanoate, $\text{Cu(CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{)}_2$, in solution.

Final answer: A: $\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4\text{(OH)}_2\text{]}$ or $\text{Cu(OH)}_2$
B: $\text{[Cu(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$
C: $\text{Cu(CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{)}_2$

hints: Think which anion must combine with $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ to make $\text{CuCO}_3(s)$ directly from $\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$.
walkthrough:
Choose the carbonate source**
To convert soluble $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ to solid $\text{CuCO}_3$ you simply supply carbonate ions. Aqueous sodium carbonate, $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$, provides $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ which precipitates $\text{CuCO}_3$.
Final answer: $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ or $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$

hints: Write the standard carbonate plus acid pattern of salt plus $\text{CO}_2$ plus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, using two $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ to match the two ethanoate groups in the product.
walkthrough:
Construct the acid carbonate equation**
Carbonate plus acid always gives salt plus carbon dioxide plus water. Here the salt is copper(II) ethanoate, so you need two ethanoic acid molecules to supply two $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^-$ groups: $\text{CuCO}_3 + 2\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H} \rightarrow \text{Cu(CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{)}_2 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.

hints: Visualise adding acid to a solid carbonate, what you would see for gas, solid and solution colour for copper.
walkthrough:
Describe what you would see**
You would see effervescence as $\text{CO}_2$ bubbles off. The solid $\text{CuCO}_3$ disappears as it dissolves, and a blue or green copper(II) solution appears.
Final answer: Any two: fizzing / bubbles / effervescence; solid disappears / dissolves; green / blue solution formed.

hints: Add up charges by assigning Pt as +2, $\text{NH}_3$ as neutral and each $\text{Cl}$ as -1.
walkthrough:
Balance metal charge with ligands**
Platinum is in oxidation state +2. Each chloride ligand carries -1, so two give -2. Ammonia is a neutral molecule with no charge. Adding them, $+2 + 0 + 2(-1) = 0$, so the overall complex has no charge.
Final answer: Pt is +2, two $\text{Cl}^-$ give -2 total and $\text{NH}_3$ is neutral, so $(+2) + 2(-1) = 0$, complex is neutral.

hints: Recall the characteristic 4 coordinate geometry of Pt(II) and what trans means for the positions of identical ligands.
Think of the bond angle between opposite ligands in that geometry.
walkthrough:
Draw the trans arrangement**
Pt(II) with coordination number 4 is square planar. Place Pt in the centre, put the two Cl ligands opposite each other and the two $\text{NH}_3$ ligands opposite each other, all at $90^{\circ}$ to neighbours. That is trans, Cl-Pt-NH3 alternating round the square.

State shape and angle**
Because opposite ligands lie in a straight line through Pt, the shape is square planar and the $\text{Cl-Pt-Cl}$ angle is $180^{\circ}$.

Final answer: Trans structure: Pt centre with Cl opposite Cl and $\text{H}_3\text{N}$ opposite $\text{H}_3\text{N}$ in one plane.
Shape: square planar, $\text{Cl-Pt-Cl}$ bond angle $180^{\circ}$.

hints: Think what large biological molecule inside the nucleus cis-platin targets after losing its chloride ligands.
Consider the consequence of that binding for copying genetic material and making new cancer cells.
walkthrough:
Bind to DNA**
Inside the cell cis-platin loses chloride and the Pt binds to nitrogen atoms on DNA bases, forming crosslinks that distort the double helix.

Block replication**
The distorted DNA cannot be correctly replicated or transcribed, so the cancer cell cannot divide and it undergoes programmed death. That is why it stops tumour growth.

Final answer: Cis-platin binds to DNA.
This prevents DNA replication / prevents cell division.

hints: Keep the two $\text{NH}_3$ ligands cis as in cis-platin and attach the single $\text{O-C(=O)-CH}_2\text{-O}$ group through both its O atoms to complete square planar coordination.
walkthrough:
Form the chelate**
Remove the two cis $\text{Cl}^-$ and replace them with the one bidentate ligand. The two $\text{NH}_3$ groups stay cis. The dicarboxylate type ligand donates through its two negatively charged O atoms, one from the carboxylate $\text{COO}^-$ and one from the alkoxide $\text{O}^-$, chelating Pt to give a square planar nedaplatin complex.
Final answer: Pt with two cis $\text{NH}_3$ ligands and chelating $^-\text{O-C(=O)-CH}_2\text{-O}^-$ bonded via the two O atoms, forming a 5 membered chelate ring, square planar at Pt.
